How to use this answer book

This book has three layers, in the order you should study them:

  1. The blueprint paper (5 June 2026) — the only Senior Officer paper already set on the confirmed 200-mark syllabus. Its question paper is followed by a complete model answer script.
  2. Predicted topics for 27 November 2026 — eight full focus-writing answers and a complete practice set in the June 2026 format (Analytical 40, Translation, Grammar, Banking, GK, Math).
  3. Earlier papers (Dec 2025, Jun 2025, 2021–2024) — more practice with full or pointer answers.

Answers are written the way a strong script looks in the hall: black ink, headings underlined in blue, one data box with its source, recommendations and a short conclusion. Pencil notes are coaching tips, not part of the answer.

Language: all model answers are in English, as requested. Questions that must be answered in Bangla in the exam carry a pencil note with the Bangla sub-headings to use.

Figures are current to 19–20 November 2026 and carry their sources. Key ones: policy rate 9.5% (cut on 30 July 2026); inflation 8.27% (Oct 2026); default loans 32.17% (Sept 2026); remittance USD 35.59 bn in FY26 (record); LDC graduation 24 Nov 2029; US tariff 10% (Section 301).

About the layout: Layout reconstructed from candidates' published descriptions of bank written-test answer scripts (cover fields, office code, black ink, self-drawn margins); no official specimen is publicly available. Contents prepared from the SOWritten repository, past papers (Satt Academy) and 15+ news sources, 19–20 November 2026.

Topic Prediction for 27 November 2026

Read this first: nobody can predict an exact essay title with 80 percent certainty, and anyone who claims to is guessing. What the evidence can support is the topic family a question will come from. The likelihoods below are estimates built from the past papers and six months of news, not guarantees.

1. Evidence used

A. Past Senior Officer papers (Satt Academy scrape, 19 Nov 2026). Focus-writing topics in the last seven SO papers:

Paper English focus Bangla focus Family
Jun 2026 SO Export diversification Fuel price hike and the economy Economy · Energy
May 2026 SO (IT) E-governance Ukraine–Iran tension and Bangladesh's strategy Technology · Global
Dec 2025 SO Digital economy and development Climate change and productivity Economy/Tech · Climate
Jun 2025 SO Microcredit and poverty Democratic movements and youth Banking · Social
May 2024 SO (IT) Technology and student achievement Heatwave and environment Technology · Climate
Jan 2022 SO 50 years of banking management Women's struggle under climate change Banking · Climate
Nov 2021 SO Banking for e-commerce COP26 and Bangladesh Banking/Tech · Climate

Findings
- 7 of 7 papers had at least one focus topic from economy, banking or technology.
- 5 of 7 had a climate, environment or energy topic, and the June 2026 Analytical question (d) was also environment versus growth.
- Topics are current: COP26 in 2021, heatwave in 2024, Ukraine–Iran and fuel prices in 2026.
- Exact titles rarely repeat within a year. Export diversification and fuel prices were asked in June 2026, so expect a different angle on the same families.

B. 2026 papers set by the same committee for other posts. Officer, Cash and IT papers in 2025–26 asked about: remittance's impact; the need for foreign-exchange reserves; eco-tourism and banks; institutional reform for democratic transition; youth and a corruption-free country; the fifth industrial revolution; agriculture; arguments on LDC graduation, trade liberalisation and LDC duty-free market access; and the socio-economic outcomes of hosting the FIFA World Cup.

C. News intensity, mid-May to mid-November 2026. Two research passes covered 14 Bangla dailies and portals (Prothom Alo, bdnews24, Ittefaq, Manab Zamin, Ajker Patrika, Bangladesh Pratidin, Bangla Tribune, Desh Rupantor, Jugantor, Kaler Kantho, Samakal, Daily Star Bangla, TBS Bangla, Bonik Barta) and international and English sources (IMF, World Bank, ADB, WTO, UNCTAD, BIS, US Fed, UN News, AP, Al Jazeera, Nikkei Asia, Bloomberg headlines, The Daily Star, Financial Express, TBS, Dhaka Tribune, UNB). Reuters, FT, The Economist and BBC Bangla could not be fetched.

The chance for any single specific title is far lower, so prepare the families, not titles.

4. Quick outlines for the remaining likely topics

Revenue mobilisation and the new IMF programme
Tax-GDP about 7%, among the lowest in the world · FY27 revenue target Tk 6.95 lakh crore (NBR Tk 6.04 lakh crore) · causes: narrow tax base, exemptions, informality, weak digital administration · the new IMF programme of USD 4.5–5 bn under negotiation (old programme exited in May 2026) · reforms: separate tax policy from administration, digital VAT, cut exemptions, a property tax, widen the income-tax net · conclusion: without revenue, no development budget is sustainable.

Institutional reform and democratic governance
2024 uprising → February 2026 election → constitutional reform committee formed 13 July 2026 · independent Election Commission, judiciary, ACC, central bank and public service · checks and balances, local government · role of youth and media · conclusion: elections are necessary but not sufficient; institutions make democracy last.

Global economy and its impact on Bangladesh
IMF: world growth 3.1% and inflation 4.7% in 2026 · oil about USD 92 after peaking above USD 120 · US tariffs and trade realignment · AI-driven trade boom (WTO 3.9% trade growth) · effects on Bangladesh: imported inflation, export demand, remittance from the Gulf · policy: diversify markets, energy security, reserve buffers.

Rohingya crisis
About 1.2 million refugees · 2026 Joint Response Plan USD 710.5 m (26% lower) · food rations cut to USD 6 for some · Arakan Army controls about 90% of Rakhine · Bangladesh holds the UNGA presidency, a diplomatic opportunity · solution: safe, voluntary, dignified return; burden-sharing; accountability at the ICJ.

5. The Analytical section (40): what to expect

Based on the June 2026 paper, expect four parts: (a) a scheduling or ranking puzzle; (b) critique a business decision (averages, correlation vs causation, capacity, sampling); (c) find the hidden assumption or what weakens or strengthens an argument; (d) arguments for and against a statement. Likely statements for (d): IMF loan with strict conditions, bank mergers, AI and jobs, environment vs growth, subsidy removal, LDC graduation timing, cashless society. Two complete practice sets are answered in this book.

6. Sources

Past papers: sattacademy.com/job-solution/combined-bank and the per-paper written-question pages (scraped 19 Nov 2026). News facts: see data/facts.json; every figure there carries its source and date.

Ans. to the Q. No. 1 — Export Diversification in Bangladesh

Export Diversification in Bangladesh: Moving Beyond a One-Product Economy

"Don't put all your eggs in one basket." — an old proverb that now describes Bangladesh's biggest export risk.

Introduction
Bangladesh has become the world's second-largest garment exporter, but this success hides a structural weakness: readymade garments (RMG) earn about 80 percent of total export receipts. When the European Union, which buys the largest share of our garments, slows down, or when a price war breaks out among Asian suppliers, the whole economy feels the shock. With graduation from the LDC group now deferred to 24 November 2029, the next three years are a narrow window to build a broader export basket.

Current picture of exports

Indicator Latest figure Source
Total exports, FY26 about USD 48 billion (−0.58%; target USD 55 bn) EPB via TBS, Jul 2026
Share of RMG in exports about 80% Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27
RMG exports, FY26 USD 38.70 billion (−1.64%) EPB via TBS, Jul 2026
Exports, Jul–Oct FY27 USD 17.04 billion (about +6%) EPB via FE, Nov 2026
US tariff on Bangladeshi goods 10% (Section 301, since 24 Jul 2026); earlier 20% reciprocal tariff struck down The Daily Star, 24 Jul 2026
Import payments, Jul–Apr FY26 USD 61.62 billion (+5.92%) Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27
LDC graduation deferred to 24 Nov 2029 UN General Assembly, Oct 2026

Why diversification is urgent
1. Concentration risk: one product and two markets mean any shock hits 80 percent of earnings at once. The EU and the USA take 67.5 percent of RMG exports, and since July 2026 the US charges a 10 percent Section 301 tariff on Bangladeshi goods.
2. Loss of preferences after 2029: duty-free access under EU "Everything But Arms" ends after graduation. The new EU GSP rules expected from 2027 tighten the safeguard on apparel, and GSP+ will demand compliance with more international labour, environment and governance conventions.
3. Stagnant export growth: FY26 exports of about USD 48 billion fell short of the USD 55 billion target, while record remittances (USD 35.59 billion) rather than exports kept the external account stable.
4. Jobs for the youth: RMG is automating; new sectors are needed to absorb about two million new job seekers every year.

Promising sectors beyond RMG
- Leather and footwear: raw material is domestic; the Savar tannery estate needs a working central effluent treatment plant to win buyer certification.
- Pharmaceuticals: already export to more than 150 countries; the TRIPS waiver continues until graduation.
- Light engineering, bicycles and electronics: strong SME base and growing demand in Europe.
- Agro-processing and frozen food: jute goods, shrimp, vegetables and processed foods.
- ICT and freelancing services: low capital need, high value added.
- Shipbuilding: small ocean-going vessels for Europe and Africa.

Main obstacles
- Bonded-warehouse and cash-incentive facilities are designed mainly for RMG.
- Energy shortages and higher fuel prices raise production costs.
- Port congestion, long lead time and weak testing and certification facilities.
- Limited access to long-term finance for new exporters, and high interest rates (the policy rate was 10 percent until July 2026 and is now 9.5 percent).
- Weak branding and few trade agreements: the first EPA, with Japan, was signed only in February 2026, and none exists yet with the EU or ASEAN.

Role of the banking sector
Banks can lead diversification by: extending bonded-warehouse-style back-to-back LC facilities to non-RMG sectors; using Bangladesh Bank's Tk 3,000 crore window for non-traditional exports and the export development fund; offering export credit guarantees for first-time exporters; and financing compliance upgrades such as effluent treatment and green factories.

Recommendations
1. Give every export sector the same bonded-warehouse and duty-drawback facilities as RMG.
2. Ratify and use the Japan EPA quickly, and negotiate FTAs/CEPAs with ASEAN, India and the Gulf before 2029.
3. Meet the 32 GSP+ conventions on labour rights, human rights, environment and governance.
4. Build product-testing labs and international certification centres.
5. Ensure gas and electricity supply to economic zones.
6. Create a "Brand Bangladesh" campaign for non-garment products.

Conclusion
Export diversification is no longer a choice but a condition for sustaining growth after LDC graduation. If policy support, bank finance and infrastructure move together, Bangladesh can turn its manufacturing strength into a broad, resilient export economy.

Ans. to the Q. No. 2 — Impact of Fuel Price Hikes on the Economy of Bangladesh

✎In the exam this answer must be written in Bangla. Use these Bangla sub-headings: ভূমিকা · জ্বালানি তেলের দাম বাড়ার প্রেক্ষাপট · সাম্প্রতিক মূল্য সমন্বয় (তথ্য-ছক) · কৃষি, শিল্প ও পরিবহনে প্রভাব · মূল্যস্ফীতি ও সাধারণ মানুষের জীবনযাত্রা · বৈদেশিক মুদ্রার রিজার্ভ ও আমদানি ব্যয় · করণীয় · উপসংহার

Impact of Fuel Price Hikes on the Economy of Bangladesh

"Energy is the golden thread that connects economic growth, social equity and environmental sustainability." — Ban Ki-moon

Introduction
Fuel oil is the lifeblood of transport, irrigation and power generation in Bangladesh. Because the country imports almost all of its petroleum, every rise in world oil prices quickly reaches the farmer's irrigation pump, the bus fare and the market price of rice. In 2026 the war in the Middle East and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz pushed global energy prices up, and the government adjusted domestic prices twice.

Recent price adjustments

Date Diesel (Tk/litre) Note
Before April 2026 100 —
April 2026 115 +Tk 15, linked to global crude prices
September 2026 135 +Tk 20 for all four fuels; petrol Tk 160

Source: Energy Division announcements reported by Dhaka Tribune and bdnews24, 2026. Diesel is about 66 percent of total fuel-oil use.

Impact on the economy
1. Inflation: transport and production costs pass into prices. Non-food inflation rose to 9.89 percent in October 2026, a 41-month high (BBS), even as food inflation eased.
2. Agriculture: diesel runs irrigation pumps and power tillers; higher costs reduce farm profit and can lower Boro rice output.
3. Transport: bus and truck fares rise, raising the cost of moving goods from farm to market.
4. Industry and exports: factories that use diesel generators face higher costs, making our exports less competitive.
5. External sector: import payments jumped 21.42 percent in April 2026 because of petroleum, LNG and fertiliser bills, putting pressure on foreign exchange reserves.
6. Poverty: fixed-income and poor households suffer most, because wage growth (7.63 percent) is lower than inflation.

Positive side
Price adjustment reduces the subsidy burden on the budget and the losses of the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation, which was losing about Tk 89 per litre of diesel, and it discourages smuggling to neighbouring countries.

Way forward
- Introduce a transparent automatic pricing formula linked to world prices.
- Give targeted diesel subsidy to farmers during the irrigation season.
- Expand domestic gas exploration and long-term LNG contracts.
- Invest in solar irrigation pumps, rooftop solar and electric public transport.
- Monitor markets to stop traders from raising prices more than costs justify.

Conclusion
Fuel prices cannot be kept artificially low forever, but sudden hikes hurt growth and the poor. A gradual, formula-based pricing policy, protection for vulnerable groups and a faster shift to renewable energy are the keys to energy security.

Ans. to the Q. No. 4 — Mathematics

(a) Minimum on-season sale of oranges
Loss in off-season = 1,800 × (11 − 8) = Tk 5,400
Overhead for 12 months = 12 × 3,000 = Tk 36,000
Profit per on-season orange = 10 − 6 = Tk 4
Let n = oranges sold in on-season. Overall profit ≥ 5,000:
4n − 5,400 − 36,000 ≥ 5,000
4n ≥ 46,400 ⇒ n ≥ 11,600
Answer: at least 11,600 oranges.

(b) Speed of the stream
Let stream speed = s km/h. Downstream speed = 10 + s, upstream = 10 − s.
Time is equal: 24/(10 + s) = 14/(10 − s)
240 − 24s = 140 + 14s ⇒ 38s = 100 ⇒ s = 50/19
Answer: 50/19 ≈ 2.63 km/h.

(c) Number of staff
Let staff = n and each bonus = x, so total = nx.
(n + 5)(x − 50) = nx ⇒ 5x − 50n = 250 ⇒ x − 10n = 50 … (i)
(n − 5)(x + 75) = nx ⇒ 75n − 5x = 375 ⇒ 15n − x = 75 … (ii)
Adding (i) and (ii): 5n = 125 ⇒ n = 25 (and x = Tk 300).
Answer: 25 staff members.

(d) The two-digit number
Let the number be 10a + b.
a + b + 7 = 3a ⇒ b = 2a − 7 … (i)
(10a + b) − 18 = 10b + a ⇒ a − b = 2 … (ii)
From (i) and (ii): a − (2a − 7) = 2 ⇒ a = 5, b = 3
Check: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15 = 3 × 5 ✓; 53 − 18 = 35 ✓
Answer: 53.

(e) Pieces of wood
Area of doors = 3 × 2 × 1.25 = 7.5 m²
Area of windows = 6 × 1 × 1.25 = 7.5 m²
Total = 15 m²; area of one piece = 5 × 0.60 = 3 m²
Pieces = 15 ÷ 3 = 5
Answer: 5 pieces.

Ans. to the Q. No. 6 — Analytical Reasoning, Critical Thinking and Argumentative Writing

(a) Interview schedule
1. C must be on Friday and E on Tuesday (given).
2. E cannot be before A, so A must come before Tuesday ⇒ A is on Monday.
3. B cannot be on Monday or Friday, and D must be immediately after B. The only free consecutive days are Wednesday and Thursday ⇒ B on Wednesday, D on Thursday.
4. Check: A (Mon) is before C (Fri) ✓.

Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday
A E B D C

(b) Critique of the CEO's decision
The CEO's conclusion is weak because it rests on one average and several hidden assumptions.
1. Average delivery time is not efficiency. It ignores cost per order, on-time rate, damage rate and customer satisfaction.
2. Different conditions. North may serve nearby urban customers while South serves remote areas; the 2-day vs 4-day gap may reflect distance, not performance.
3. Averages hide variation. South may deliver most orders in 2 days with a few very late ones that pull the average up.
4. Capacity constraint. Shifting 80 percent of volume to North may overload its staff, trucks and storage, so its delivery time will rise, possibly above 4 days.
5. "Twice as efficient" is a misuse of ratio. Halving time does not double efficiency in cost or quality terms.
6. Geography. Customers near South would face longer distances if served from North.

Better decision: compare cost per delivery, on-time percentage and capacity utilisation for similar customer zones; find why South is slower; then improve South or shift volume gradually through a pilot while monitoring results.

(c) Implied assumption
The economist assumes that if deposits were not insured, depositors would be able to judge (and would actually take the trouble to judge) how secure a bank is, and would move their money accordingly, so that this market discipline would force banks to be safer. In short, bank failures are at least partly caused by risky behaviour that depositor scrutiny could prevent.

(d) Environmental protection vs economic growth

Arguments that environmental protection is more important
1. Growth that destroys rivers, forests and air reduces future growth; environmental damage costs Bangladesh a large share of GDP through floods, salinity and pollution.
2. Bangladesh is among the most climate-vulnerable countries; protection is a matter of survival.
3. Health costs of pollution reduce labour productivity.
4. Global buyers and lenders now demand green compliance; protection keeps export markets open.

Arguments that economic growth is more important
1. A lower-middle-income country must create jobs for millions of young people and reduce poverty first.
2. Growth provides the revenue and technology needed to protect the environment later.
3. Strict rules may raise costs and drive away investment.

Rebuttal and position
The choice is false. Countries that grew first and cleaned up later paid a far higher cost, while green growth (renewable energy, green factories, sustainable finance) now creates jobs itself. Bangladesh already has more than 200 LEED-certified green garment factories, showing that environmental standards and export growth can go together.
Position: Environmental protection should not be sacrificed for growth; the goal is green and sustainable growth, supported by green banking, carbon pricing over time and enforcement of the Environment Conservation Act.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. — Non-Performing Loans and Banking Sector Reform in Bangladesh

Default Loans and the Road to Banking Sector Reform

"A bank is only as strong as the trust of its depositors."

Introduction
Banks are the heart of an economy: they collect savings and pump credit into business. In Bangladesh that heart is weak. In June 2026, defaulted loans reached about Tk 6.06 lakh crore, or 32.78 percent of all loans, which IMF data show is the highest ratio in the world. The Governor himself said in November 2026 that about one-third of the sector's money had been "stolen". Restoring the health of banks is now the most urgent economic reform.

The magnitude of the problem

Indicator Figure Source
Default loans, June 2026 about Tk 6.06 lakh crore (32.78%) Bangladesh Bank via Prothom Alo
Default loans, Sept 2026 (latest) Tk 5.97 lakh crore (32.17%) Finance Minister in Parliament, 16 Nov 2026
Private credit growth, Sept 2026 4.17% (record low) Bangladesh Bank via Samakal
Default ratio, state-owned banks 43.2% Financial Express
Default ratio, Dec 2024 20.20% Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27
Five merged Islamic banks 84.22% of loans in default 2026 reports
Money stuck in money loan courts about Tk 6.48 lakh crore Daily Sun, Sep 2026

Causes
1. Political and insider lending: loans approved on influence, not on business merit; some groups captured whole banks.
2. Wilful default: a culture where large borrowers expect rescheduling and write-offs.
3. Weak supervision: regulatory forbearance and repeated relaxation of loan-classification rules hid the real picture for years.
4. Slow legal process: money loan court cases drag on for years.
5. Board-level governance failure: directors interfering in credit decisions.

Consequences
Capital shortfalls and liquidity crises in weak banks; loss of depositor confidence; private-sector credit growth falling to a record-low 4.17 percent in September 2026; higher lending rates for honest borrowers; and pressure on the budget for recapitalisation (Tk 36,706 crore set aside in FY27 for bank restructuring).

Reforms under way
- Bank Resolution Act 2026: a legal framework to merge, restructure or close failing banks. Section 18A, which allowed former owners to reclaim banks, was repealed in September 2026.
- Sammilito Islami Bank: five troubled Shariah banks merged into one state-owned bank with Tk 20,000 crore government capital.
- Deposit Protection Act 2026: insurance coverage doubled from Tk 1 lakh to Tk 2 lakh per depositor.
- Asset Quality Reviews and a move to Expected Credit Loss (IFRS 9) provisioning by 2027.
- Recovery of laundered money: about Tk 70,446 crore of assets frozen or attached at home and abroad.

Recommendations
1. Publish a list of wilful defaulters and bar them from new credit, foreign travel and company directorships.
2. Set up special benches to settle large money-loan cases within a fixed time.
3. Pass the Distressed Asset Management Act to create an asset management company for bad loans.
4. Apply "fit and proper" tests to bank directors and limit family control of boards.
5. Give Bangladesh Bank full operational independence in supervision.
6. Merge banks only after independent asset-quality reviews and with fresh management, so that mergers do not spread the infection.

Conclusion
Bangladesh cannot reach its growth targets with a banking system in which one taka in every three lent is not being repaid. The new laws are a start, but their success depends on consistent enforcement, regardless of who the defaulter is.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. — LDC Graduation Deferred to 2029: Opportunities and Challenges

Using the Extra Three Years: Bangladesh's LDC Graduation Strategy

"Graduation is not the end of the journey; it is the start of a new one."

Introduction
On 29 October 2026 the UN General Assembly, through resolution A/81/L.8 adopted without objection, deferred Bangladesh's graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category from 24 November 2026 to 24 November 2029, granting the request of the new government. Nepal received the same extension. The decision gives Bangladesh three more years of trade preferences, but also three fewer excuses.

Background
Bangladesh met all three graduation criteria (per-capita income, human assets and economic vulnerability) in the 2018 and 2021 reviews. The government argued that the preparatory period was disrupted by the pandemic, the 2024 political transition and global shocks such as the Middle East war.

Why the deferral helps
1. Preferences continue: duty-free, quota-free access to the EU under "Everything But Arms" and preferential treatment in other markets remain until 2029.
2. Pharmaceutical patents: the TRIPS waiver lets local firms keep producing generic medicines.
3. Concessional finance: access to cheaper loans continues.
4. Time to reform: the economy is weak (FY27 growth forecasts 3.2–4.0 percent) and the banking sector is stressed. Graduating now could have added a fresh shock.

Challenges that remain
- Exports are concentrated: about 80 percent comes from RMG.
- The new EU GSP rules expected from 2027 tighten the safeguard on apparel, where Bangladesh's share is very large, and GSP+ will demand more international conventions.
- The EU called the extension an "exceptional time-bound" measure that must be "accompanied by concrete, measurable domestic actions" (UN General Assembly, October 2026).
- The US now charges a 10 percent Section 301 tariff on Bangladeshi goods.
- A UN assessment estimated export losses of more than USD 17.5 billion a year after graduation without preferences.
- Low revenue (about 7 percent of GDP) limits investment in skills and infrastructure.

Opportunities to seize
Better credit rating and branding as a graduating economy; more FDI (USD 1.78 billion in 2025, up 45 percent, according to UNCTAD); and a chance to negotiate new trade deals. The EPA with Japan, signed in February 2026, is the first such deal.

What must be done before 2029
1. Prepare to qualify for EU GSP+ by implementing labour, environment and human-rights conventions.
2. Sign FTAs or CEPAs with ASEAN, India, China and the Gulf, and ratify the Japan EPA.
3. Diversify exports: leather, pharmaceuticals, light engineering, agro-processing and ICT services.
4. Raise revenue through tax reform and digital tax administration.
5. Upgrade ports, power supply and logistics to cut lead time.
6. Upskill workers for higher-value manufacturing.

Conclusion
The deferral is a breathing space, not a holiday. If Bangladesh uses these three years for real reform, it will graduate in 2029 as a confident, competitive economy rather than a vulnerable one.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. — Stagflation Risk: High Inflation, Slowing Growth and the Policy Response

Between Inflation and Stagnation: Bangladesh's Policy Dilemma

"Inflation is taxation without legislation." — Milton Friedman

Introduction
Bangladesh faces an uncomfortable mix: inflation has stayed above 8 percent for more than two years, while growth has slowed to its weakest level in decades. This combination of high prices and low growth, called stagflation, squeezes household incomes and discourages investment.

The picture in numbers

Indicator Figure Source
Inflation, October 2026 8.27% (food 6.40%, non-food 9.89%) BBS
Wage growth, October 2026 7.63% (below inflation) BBS
GDP growth, FY26 (revised) 3.68% BBS
FY27 growth forecasts IMF 3.2%, World Bank 3.4%, ADB 4.0% IMF, World Bank, ADB
Policy rate 9.5% (cut from 10% in July 2026) Bangladesh Bank
Poverty rate, 2026 22.5% (18.7% in 2022) World Bank

Causes
1. Cost-push factors: fuel price hikes (diesel up from Tk 100 to Tk 135 in 2026), LNG shortages and costly imports after the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz.
2. Exchange-rate pass-through: the taka's depreciation since 2022 raised import costs.
3. Market syndicates and supply-chain weaknesses in essential commodities.
4. Investment drought: high interest rates, weak banks, energy shortages and political uncertainty kept private credit growth near 5 percent.
5. Government borrowing from banks crowded out private credit.

Policy response
- Monetary policy: Bangladesh Bank kept the policy rate at 10 percent for almost two years. With food inflation falling, it cut the rate to 9.5 percent in July 2026 to revive credit, while holding it there in the first quarterly MPS.
- Fiscal policy: the FY27 budget (Tk 9.38 lakh crore) cut duties on essentials, introduced family and farmer cards, and kept the deficit at 3.6 percent of GDP.
- Stimulus: a Tk 60,000 crore refinance and pre-finance package targets CMSMEs, agriculture and closed factories, aiming at about 25 lakh jobs.
- IMF talks: a new USD 4.5–5 billion programme is being negotiated.

Why tight money alone is not enough
Most of today's inflation comes from costs and supply, not excess demand. Raising rates further would hurt investment without bringing down fuel, freight or food prices. Monetary and fiscal policy must act together.

Recommendations
1. Coordinate monetary and fiscal policy; avoid financing deficits through bank borrowing.
2. Break market syndicates through competition law and more importers.
3. Protect the poor with targeted cash transfers rather than blanket subsidies.
4. Restore energy supply through long-term LNG deals and renewables.
5. Clean up banks so that lower policy rates actually reach productive borrowers.

Conclusion
Escaping stagflation needs patience and coordination: steady disinflation through supply-side fixes, combined with targeted support to restart investment and jobs.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. — Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Banking in Bangladesh

AI in Banking: Opportunity, Risk and Responsibility

"Banking is no longer somewhere you go, but something you do." — Brett King

Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how banks lend, serve customers and fight fraud. The IMF chief called AI "a slow-moving tsunami" that could affect about 40 percent of jobs worldwide. For Bangladeshi banks, AI is both a tool for efficiency and inclusion and a source of new risks.

Uses of AI in banking
1. Credit scoring: using transaction and mobile data to lend to farmers and small entrepreneurs who have no collateral or credit history.
2. Fraud detection and AML: machine learning flags suspicious transactions faster than manual checks, supporting BFIU's work against money laundering.
3. Customer service: chatbots and voice assistants in Bangla serve customers 24/7.
4. e-KYC: facial recognition with NID makes account opening quick.
5. Risk management: early-warning systems can predict loan default, which is vital when default loans exceed 32 percent.

Bangladesh's digital foundation

Initiative Status (2026) Source
Bangla QR Mandatory single merchant QR since 1 Jul 2026; zero interchange fee from 1 Oct Bangladesh Bank
Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS) Targeted for July 2027 (Gates Foundation's Mojaloop support) Bangladesh Bank via Dhaka Tribune, Nov 2026
Digital nano-loans Refinance scheme extended to June 2028 Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27
Digital bank licences No final decision yet 2026 reports

Risks and challenges
- Cyber security: AI can also be used by criminals for deepfake fraud and phishing. The 2016 reserve heist shows the cost of weak security.
- Bias and fairness: algorithms trained on biased data may exclude women or rural borrowers.
- Data privacy: Bangladesh still needs a strong data-protection law.
- Jobs: routine back-office and teller jobs may decline. Global banks are cutting junior analyst intake, though S&P Global sees no near-term mass layoffs.
- Skills gap: few bankers are trained in data science.

Recommendations
1. Bangladesh Bank should issue AI governance guidelines on explainability, fairness and human oversight.
2. Enact a data-protection law and strengthen bank cyber-security standards.
3. Retrain staff for relationship management, data analysis and cyber security.
4. Use AI first for inclusion (credit for CMSMEs) and anti-fraud, not only for cost-cutting.
5. Use regulatory sandboxes, through the Regulatory FinTech Facilitation Office, to test innovations safely.

Conclusion
AI will not replace bankers, but bankers who use AI will replace those who do not. With sound regulation and training, AI can make Bangladesh's banks safer, faster and more inclusive.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. — Remittance: Lifeline of the Economy and the Fight Against Hundi

Record Remittances and the Fight Against Hundi

"Remittance is the silent engine of Bangladesh's economy."

Introduction
More than a crore of Bangladeshis work abroad, and the money they send home has become the strongest pillar of the external sector. In FY26 remittances reached a record USD 35.59 billion, up 17.3 percent, while export earnings stagnated.

Data box

Indicator Figure Source
Remittance, FY26 USD 35.59 bn (+17.3%), record Bangladesh Bank via FE
Remittance, FY27 to 16 Nov USD 13.43 bn (+13.4%) Bangladesh Bank via UNB
Exports, Jul–Oct FY27 USD 17.04 bn (+6%) EPB via TBS, Nov 2026
Top source country, FY26 Saudi Arabia (USD 5.84 bn) Bangladesh Bank
Gross reserves, 19 Nov 2026 USD 34.38 bn (BPM6: 29.57 bn) Bangladesh Bank via BSS
FY27 projection USD 38.72 bn Finance Division MTMPS

Why remittance matters
1. Reserves and exchange rate: remittances financed the trade gap and stabilised the taka around Tk 122–125 per dollar (Tk 124.70 on 19 November 2026).
2. Rural consumption and poverty reduction: families spend on food, education, health and housing.
3. Investment: some remittance goes into small businesses, land and savings instruments.

Why the surge happened
A market-based exchange rate narrowed the gap between official and hundi rates. Stricter action against money laundering after 2024 and easier digital channels also helped.

The hundi problem
Hundi is an informal transfer system: the worker pays an agent abroad and the family receives taka at home, but no dollars enter the country. It drains reserves and is linked to money laundering and capital flight. A white paper estimated USD 234 billion was laundered from Bangladesh between 2009 and 2023.

Challenges
High migration costs, unskilled migrants earning low wages, dependence on the Gulf (now affected by war), and the risk that inflows slow down after the recent surge.

Recommendations
1. Keep the exchange rate market-based so that formal channels stay competitive.
2. Expand digital remittance through MFS and bank apps, with instant credit to family accounts.
3. Cut migration costs and fight fraudulent recruiting agents.
4. Send skilled workers (nurses, technicians, IT) to new markets such as Japan and Europe.
5. Offer remittance bonds and investment schemes for expatriates.
6. Let BFIU continue strict action against hundi networks.

Conclusion
Remittance has carried the economy through a difficult period. Making the formal channel the easiest and cheapest choice, and sending more skilled workers, will keep this lifeline strong.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. (Bangla focus) — Climate Finance, COP31 and Bangladesh

✎Write this in Bangla in the exam. Bangla sub-headings: ভূমিকা · বাংলাদেশের জলবায়ু ঝুঁকি · COP31 ও বাংলাদেশের দাবি · লস অ্যান্ড ড্যামেজ তহবিল: প্রতিশ্রুতি বনাম বাস্তবতা · ঋণ নয়, অনুদান · গ্রিন ব্যাংকিং ও টেকসই অর্থায়ন · করণীয় · উপসংহার

Climate Finance and Bangladesh: Expectations from COP31

Introduction
Bangladesh emits less than 0.5 percent of global greenhouse gases, yet it is among the countries hit hardest by climate change. At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye (9–20 November 2026), Bangladesh's delegation, led by the Prime Minister, demanded fair and accessible climate finance.

Bangladesh's climate burden
Bangladesh estimates its annual climate losses at about USD 15.2 billion, from floods, cyclones, salinity, river erosion and heatwaves. Flash floods in 2026 damaged crops and pushed food prices up.

Promise vs reality

Item Figure Source
Loss and Damage Fund about USD 600 m received vs USD 2.8 bn requested by 119 countries Climate Action Network, 15 Nov 2026
Adaptation Fund pledges at COP31 USD 50 m vs USD 300 m annual floor Climate Action Network, 18 Nov 2026
Global climate finance gap up to USD 840 bn a year short of the USD 1.3 trn goal UN News, 13 Nov 2026
Renewable-energy climate finance to Bangladesh 90.4% given as loans UNB, Nov 2026

Bangladesh's key demands
1. Grants, not loans, for adaptation and loss and damage. Loans add debt to victims.
2. Simple, direct access to funds for vulnerable countries and local communities.
3. More finance for adaptation, not only mitigation.
4. Technology transfer for renewable energy.

Role of banks: green banking
Bangladesh Bank's sustainable finance policy requires banks to finance green projects (solar, energy-efficient factories, effluent treatment). Banks can issue green bonds and sukuk, price climate risk into lending, and expand refinance for solar irrigation.

What Bangladesh must do at home
Implement the National Adaptation Plan; build climate-resilient infrastructure; scale up renewable energy to reduce dependence on imported fuel; and improve transparency so that climate funds reach the people who need them.

Conclusion
Climate justice means the polluters pay. Bangladesh must keep pressing for grant-based finance while showing, through strong domestic action, that every dollar received is used well.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. (Bangla focus) — Energy Security of Bangladesh amid the Middle East Crisis

✎Write this in Bangla in the exam. Bangla sub-headings: ভূমিকা · মধ্যপ্রাচ্য যুদ্ধ ও হরমুজ প্রণালী · আমদানিনির্ভর জ্বালানি খাত · গ্যাস ও বিদ্যুৎ সংকট (তথ্য-ছক) · অর্থনীতিতে প্রভাব · নবায়নযোগ্য জ্বালানির সম্ভাবনা · করণীয় · উপসংহার

Energy Security of Bangladesh amid the Middle East Crisis

Introduction
Energy security means a reliable supply of energy at an affordable price. The war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, and the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has shown how fragile Bangladesh's import-dependent energy system is.

The shock in numbers

Indicator Figure Source
Brent crude, 19 Nov 2026 about USD 92/barrel (above USD 100 at the peak) oilprice.com
Spot LNG price USD 24–28/MMBtu (about USD 10 before the war) bdnews24
Gas supply vs demand 2,624 vs about 3,800 mmcfd bdnews24
Rural load-shedding, August 2026 8–10 hours a day 2026 reports
Diesel price Tk 100 → Tk 135 per litre in 2026 Dhaka Tribune

Impact
A fire at the Moheshkhali floating LNG terminal on 21 July pushed load-shedding above 2,500 MW and hit about 2,500 factories. Irrigation costs rose, fuel and transport costs pushed non-food inflation near 10 percent, and the import bill strained reserves. QatarEnergy's force majeure halved LNG deliveries.

Root causes of vulnerability
Declining domestic gas fields, slow exploration, over-reliance on imported LNG and oil, and a slow shift to renewables.

Way forward
1. Intensify domestic gas exploration, onshore and offshore, through BAPEX and international partners.
2. Diversify LNG sources through long-term contracts with several suppliers.
3. Scale up solar (rooftop, irrigation, utility-scale) and wind.
4. Improve energy efficiency in industry and buildings.
5. Build strategic oil reserves for at least 60 days.
6. Use a transparent fuel-pricing formula with targeted support for farmers.

Conclusion
Energy security is national security. Bangladesh must turn this crisis into a push for domestic gas and renewable energy, so that the next global shock does not switch off its factories.

Ans. to the Predicted Q. (Bangla focus) — Youth Unemployment and Skills Development

✎Write this in Bangla in the exam. Bangla sub-headings: ভূমিকা · তরুণ জনগোষ্ঠী: সম্ভাবনা ও ঝুঁকি · শিক্ষিত বেকারত্বের কারণ · চতুর্থ শিল্পবিপ্লব ও দক্ষতার ঘাটতি · কর্মসংস্থান সৃষ্টিতে ব্যাংকের ভূমিকা · করণীয় · উপসংহার

Youth Unemployment and Skills Development in Bangladesh

Introduction
About two million young people enter Bangladesh's labour market every year. With growth slowing (FY26: 3.68 percent) and private investment weak, many educated youths cannot find suitable jobs. This is a "demographic dividend" at risk of becoming a burden.

Causes
1. Skills mismatch: degrees do not match what employers need, such as technical, digital and language skills.
2. Slow job creation: weak investment, energy shortages and the banking crisis limit new factories.
3. Automation in garments and services.
4. Weak technical and vocational education (TVET).
5. Limited access to finance for young entrepreneurs.

Opportunities
IT and freelancing, the care economy, agro-processing, light engineering, overseas employment of skilled workers, and the green economy (solar installation, recycling).

Role of banks
Collateral-free start-up loans; Bangladesh Bank's Tk 60,000 crore stimulus, which includes windows for youth employment and CMSMEs; the new venture-capital platform launched by banks (reported as Bangladesh Startup Investment Company); and digital nano-loans.

Recommendations
1. Reform the curriculum with industry participation; expand apprenticeships.
2. Make TVET attractive and of high quality.
3. Create a national job-matching platform.
4. Support start-ups through venture capital, incubators and easy registration.
5. Train youth in languages and certified skills for overseas jobs.

Conclusion
The youth led Bangladesh's political change in 2024; now they need an economy that can use their talent. Skills, finance and investment together can turn a jobless generation into the engine of growth.

Practice Set in the June 2026 Format — Questions and Model Answers

The June 2026 Analytical question had four parts: (a) a logic or scheduling puzzle, (b) critique a decision, (c) find the hidden assumption, (d) arguments for and against. Expect the same four types on 27 November. Both puzzles below have been checked by computer to have exactly one solution.

Ans. to the Practice Q. No. 6 (Set 1) — Analytical Reasoning (40)

(a) Question: Six loan files — P, Q, R, S, T and U — are reviewed one per day from Monday to Saturday. S is reviewed on Wednesday. P is reviewed before S, but not on Monday. T is reviewed after S. Q is reviewed on the day immediately after T. U is reviewed after Q. R is not reviewed on Saturday. Determine the schedule.

Answer:
1. S is on Wednesday, and P is before S but not on Monday, so P is on Tuesday.
2. T is after S, Q immediately follows T, and U comes after Q. The only three days after Wednesday are Thursday, Friday and Saturday, so T = Thursday, Q = Friday, U = Saturday.
3. Only Monday is left, so R = Monday. R is not on Saturday ✓.

Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
R P S T Q U

(b) Question: A bank's marketing head reports that branches which ran a television advertisement grew deposits by 15 percent last year, while branches without the advertisement grew by only 5 percent. He concludes that the advertisement caused the extra growth and proposes tripling the advertising budget. Critique this decision.

Answer: The conclusion confuses correlation with causation.
1. Selection bias: the advertised branches may be in cities where income and remittance inflows are already higher.
2. Other causes: a higher deposit rate, new products or a new branch manager may explain the growth.
3. Timing: a festival season or remittance surge (FY26 remittances +17.3 percent) may have lifted all deposits.
4. Diminishing returns: tripling the budget will not triple the effect; the same customers see the same advertisement.
5. Cost-benefit: the decision ignores whether the extra deposits are worth the cost of advertising.

Better approach: run a controlled test in similar branches, compare like with like, and measure cost per taka of new deposits before scaling up.

(c) Question: "Bangladesh Bank has cut the policy rate from 10 percent to 9.5 percent. Private investment will therefore rise, because businesses borrow more when credit is cheaper." What is the implied assumption?

Answer: The argument assumes that the main reason businesses are not investing is the high cost of credit, and that banks will pass the lower rate on to borrowers. If the real obstacles are energy shortages, political uncertainty or weak banks unwilling to lend, the rate cut will not raise investment. Private credit growth was a record-low 4.17 percent in September 2026, even after the cut.

(d) Question: Provide arguments for and against: "Bangladesh should accept a new IMF loan programme even with strict conditions."

Answer:
For:
1. It provides USD 4.5–5 billion in budget and reserve support at low cost when reserves are under pressure (BPM6 about USD 30 billion).
2. An IMF programme signals credibility and unlocks financing from the World Bank, ADB and Japan.
3. The conditions push reforms that Bangladesh needs anyway: banking clean-up, revenue (tax-GDP only about 7 percent) and a flexible exchange rate.

Against:
1. Conditions such as subsidy cuts and higher fuel prices can hurt the poor during high inflation.
2. Reforms imposed from outside may lack national ownership and be reversed.
3. The previous programme (USD 4.7 billion, raised to USD 5.5 billion) stalled, and its targets, such as cutting default loans to 10 percent, were missed. Signing a programme is not the same as reforming.

Position: Accept the programme, but negotiate the sequencing. Protect social spending, phase energy-price adjustments, and own the reform agenda so that the programme supports national priorities rather than dictating them.

Ans. to the Practice Q. No. 6 (Set 2) — Analytical Reasoning (40)

(a) Question: Five officers — Rafi, Sumi, Tanvir, Nila and Omar — are ranked from 1 (highest sales) to 5. Nila ranks higher than Rafi, and Rafi ranks higher than Sumi. Omar ranks third. Tanvir is neither first nor last. Rafi is not second. Find the ranking.

Answer:
1. Omar is 3rd. Tanvir is not 1st or 5th, so Tanvir is 2nd or 4th.
2. Nila > Rafi > Sumi, and Rafi is not 2nd, so Rafi must be 4th (3rd is taken). Then Sumi is 5th.
3. Tanvir must be 2nd (4th is taken), so Nila is 1st.

Ranking: 1 Nila, 2 Tanvir, 3 Omar, 4 Rafi, 5 Sumi.

(b) Question: After 100 CCTV cameras were installed in a market area, reported crimes rose by 20 percent. A councillor concludes that the cameras increased crime and should be removed. Critique the conclusion.

Answer: Cameras increase detection and reporting, not necessarily crime. Victims report more when evidence exists, and police record more incidents. Other factors such as population growth, economic hardship or a new reporting system may also explain the rise. The correct measures are conviction rates, serious-crime trends and comparison with similar areas without cameras. Removing the cameras on this evidence would be a mistake.

(c) Question: "Mobile financial service accounts in Bangladesh now outnumber adults, so financial inclusion of the poor has been achieved." Which fact would most weaken this argument?

Answer: The argument is weakened if many accounts are inactive or duplicates, for example one person holding several accounts, or accounts used only to receive transfers and immediately cash out. In that case account numbers overstate real inclusion, which means regular saving, borrowing and insurance by poor people. The freezing of more than 80,000 MFS accounts used for hundi and gambling in 2026 shows that account counts alone can mislead.

(d) Question: Provide arguments for and against: "Merging weak banks with stronger banks is the best solution to Bangladesh's banking crisis."

Answer:
For: it protects depositors quickly; achieves economies of scale; and avoids the panic of a bank closure. Sammilito Islami Bank, formed from five banks in 2026, began repaying depositors in September.
Against: it can spread bad loans to healthy banks; rewards the owners who looted banks (moral hazard); and does not fix the root cause, which is political lending and weak supervision. The five merged banks had about 86 percent of their Tk 1.92 lakh crore loans in default.
Position: Merger is a tool, not the solution. It must follow an independent asset-quality review, remove the old owners, bring in new management, and be combined with legal action to recover stolen money.

# Question Model answer Rule
a Replace the verb with a group verb: "The meeting was postponed." The meeting was put off. group verb
b Sentence type: "Although prices fell, people did not feel relief because wages stayed low." Complex sentence (one main clause + two subordinate clauses) sentence structure
c Meaning of "a blessing in disguise" Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good. idiom
d Passive: "The bank will open a new branch next month." A new branch will be opened by the bank next month. voice
e Indirect speech: He said to me, "Have you submitted the form?" He asked me if I had submitted the form. speech
f Identify the non-finite verb: "She wants to join a bank." "to join" (infinitive) finite / non-finite
g Correct the error: "Each of the officers have a laptop." Each of the officers has a laptop. subject-verb agreement
h Right form: "It is high time we (take) action." It is high time we took action. right form of verb
i Identify the clause: "I know that he is honest." Noun clause (object of "know") clause & phrase
j Meaning of "to burn the candle at both ends" To work too hard, from early morning till late night, and exhaust oneself. idiom

Ans. to the Practice Q. No. 9 — Financial and Banking Knowledge (10)

(a) SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio): the share of a bank's deposits that must be held in liquid assets such as cash, gold and government securities.
(b) Repo: a short-term loan from the central bank to a bank against government securities; its rate is the policy rate, now 9.5 percent in Bangladesh.
(c) NPL (non-performing loan): a loan whose principal or interest is overdue beyond the classification period (generally 90 days). Bangladesh's ratio was 32.17 percent in September 2026.
(d) CRAR under Basel III: the minimum capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 10 percent plus a 2.5 percent conservation buffer, i.e. 12.5 percent.
(e) Letter of credit (LC): a bank's written undertaking to pay the exporter on behalf of the importer when documents conform to the LC terms (governed by UCP 600).
(f) KYC: "Know Your Customer", the process of verifying a customer's identity and risk profile when opening and running an account.
(g) BFIU: Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit, which receives suspicious transaction reports and fights money laundering and terrorist financing.
(h) Deposit insurance: under the Deposit Protection Act 2026, each depositor is protected up to Tk 2 lakh if a bank fails.
(i) Bancassurance: selling insurance products through a bank's branches and customer base.
(j) Expected credit loss (ECL): IFRS 9 provisioning that requires banks to set aside money for expected future loan losses, not just losses that have already occurred.

Ans. to the Practice Q. No. 4 — Mathematics (30): Past Senior Officer Questions with Full Solutions

(a) Sonali Bank SO 2019. A and B are two stations 390 km apart. A train starts from A at 10 a.m. at 65 km/h towards B; another starts from B at 11 a.m. at 35 km/h towards A. When do they meet?
By 11 a.m. the first train covers 65 km; remaining = 325 km. Relative speed = 65 + 35 = 100 km/h. Time = 3.25 h = 3 h 15 min after 11 a.m.
Answer: 2:15 p.m.

(b) Combined 8 Bank SO 2019. A can contains liquids A and B in the ratio 7 : 5. When 9 litres of mixture are drawn off and the can is filled with B, the ratio becomes 7 : 9. How much A was there initially?
Let the mixture be 12k litres (A = 7k, B = 5k). The 9 litres drawn contain A = 21/4 and B = 15/4.
(7k − 21/4) : (5k − 15/4 + 9) = 7 : 9
9(7k − 21/4) = 7(5k + 21/4) ⇒ 63k − 189/4 = 35k + 147/4 ⇒ 28k = 84 ⇒ k = 3
Answer: A = 7 × 3 = 21 litres.

(c) Combined 6 Banks & 2 FIs SO 2019. At a certain compound rate a sum becomes 8 times in 3 years. In how many years will it become 16 times?
(1 + r)³ = 8 = 2³ ⇒ 1 + r = 2. Then (1 + r)ⁿ = 16 = 2⁴ ⇒ n = 4 years.

(d) Combined 6 Banks & 2 FIs SO 2019. A 15 km road is to be built in 300 days by 45 men. After 100 days, 2.5 km is complete. How many extra men are needed to finish on time?
Man-days per km = (45 × 100) ÷ 2.5 = 1,800. Remaining 12.5 km needs 12.5 × 1,800 = 22,500 man-days in 200 days ⇒ 112.5 men, i.e. 113 men.
Answer: 113 − 45 = 68 extra men.

(e) Rupali Bank SO 2019. A and B together can do a work in 30 days. A works 16 days, then B finishes the rest in 44 days. How long will B alone take?
30A + 30B = 16A + 44B ⇒ 14A = 14B ⇒ A = B. Together they take 30 days, so each alone takes 60 days.
Answer: 60 days.

(খ) একটি নির্দিষ্ট পরিমাণ টাকা কিছু লোকের মধ্যে এমনভাবে ভাগ করা হলো যে, ৪ জন লোক বেশি হলে প্রত্যেকে ১৬ টাকা কম পেত, আর ৪ জন কম হলে প্রত্যেকে ২৪ টাকা বেশি পেত। লোকের সংখ্যা কত?
(গ) একজন বিক্রয় প্রতিনিধির মাসিক বেতন ৫,০০০ টাকা। ৬০,০০০ টাকার বেশি বিক্রয়ের উপর ৮% এবং ৬০,০০০ টাকা পর্যন্ত বিক্রয়ে ৫% কমিশন পান। মাসিক বিক্রয় ১,০০,০০০ টাকা অতিক্রম করলে ১,০০০ টাকা বোনাস পান। কোনো মাসে মোট আয় ১০,৪০০ টাকা হলে মোট বিক্রয় কত?
(ঘ) একটি ঝুড়িতে ৪টি লাল, ৫টি নীল এবং ৩টি সবুজ বল আছে। প্রতিস্থাপন ছাড়া দুটি বল তোলা হলো। বল দুটি ভিন্ন রঙের হওয়ার সম্ভাবনা কত?
(ঙ) একটি আয়তক্ষেত্রের পরিসীমা ৬৬ সেমি। এর দৈর্ঘ্য প্রস্থের দ্বিগুণের চেয়ে ৬ সেমি বেশি। দৈর্ঘ্য নির্ণয় করো।

Ans. to the Q. No. 1 — The Role of Digital Economy in Economic Development

Digital Economy: The New Engine of Bangladesh's Development

"The digital economy is the economy." — Don Tapscott (paraphrased)

Introduction
A digital economy is the part of economic activity that runs on digital technology: online payments, e-commerce, mobile financial services, software exports, platform work and digital public services. For a populous, young country like Bangladesh, it can cut transaction costs, include the unbanked and create jobs that do not need large capital.

Bangladesh's digital economy at a glance

Indicator Status Source
National interoperable QR "Bangla QR" mandatory; closed-loop QR phased out by 30 June 2026 Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27
Instant payments Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS) targeted for July 2027 (Gates Foundation's Mojaloop support) Bangladesh Bank via Dhaka Tribune, Nov 2026
Digital nano-loans Refinance scheme extended to June 2028 Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27
Financial literacy 5,531 programmes reached 2.85 lakh people in 2025 Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27

How the digital economy drives development
1. Financial inclusion: mobile financial services and agent banking bring rural people, women and small traders into the formal system; digital nano-loans give collateral-free credit.
2. Productivity: digital payments, e-procurement and online tax filing reduce time, cost and leakage.
3. Employment: software firms, IT-enabled services and online freelancing employ hundreds of thousands of young people and earn foreign exchange.
4. Market access for SMEs: e-commerce and social commerce let small producers sell nationwide and abroad.
5. Transparency and governance: digital trails reduce corruption in public services and social safety-net payments.
6. Remittances: digital channels make formal remittance faster and cheaper than hundi.

Challenges
- Digital divide between urban and rural areas and between men and women.
- Cyber-attacks and fraud; the 2016 reserve heist remains a warning.
- Weak data-protection law and consumer protection in e-commerce.
- High internet cost and unstable connectivity outside cities.
- Shortage of skilled ICT workforce.

Role of banks
Banks must lead with secure digital banking, interoperable payments (Bangla QR, IIPS), cyber-security investment, e-KYC for easy account opening, and credit scoring based on digital transaction data for SMEs.

Recommendations
1. Enact and enforce a comprehensive data-protection law.
2. Reduce internet cost and expand rural broadband.
3. Train youth in AI, data analytics and cyber security.
4. Make all government payments and services digital end-to-end.
5. Build a national cyber-security response team for the financial sector.

Conclusion
The digital economy can help Bangladesh move from a low-cost manufacturing economy to a knowledge-based, inclusive one. Success depends on trust: secure systems, protected data and digitally skilled people.

Ans. to the Q. No. 2 — Climate Change and the Productivity of Bangladesh

✎Write this in Bangla in the exam. Bangla sub-headings: ভূমিকা · জলবায়ু পরিবর্তনের বাস্তবতা · কৃষি উৎপাদনশীলতায় প্রভাব · শ্রম উৎপাদনশীলতা ও তাপপ্রবাহ · শিল্প ও অবকাঠামো · স্বাস্থ্য ও অভিবাসন · করণীয় (অভিযোজন, সবুজ অর্থায়ন) · উপসংহার

Climate Change and the Productivity of Bangladesh

"We are the first generation to feel the effect of climate change and the last generation who can do something about it." — Barack Obama

Introduction
Bangladesh contributes very little to global emissions but is one of the countries most exposed to climate change. Rising temperature, erratic rainfall, salinity, floods and cyclones are already reducing the productivity of land, labour and capital.

Impact on productivity
1. Agriculture: salinity in the coastal belt, untimely rain and flash floods damage Boro and Aman crops. In 2026, crop losses from flash floods added to food prices (Bangladesh Bank, MPS H1FY27).
2. Labour productivity: heatwaves reduce working hours for farmers, construction workers and garment workers; heat stress lowers output per hour.
3. Industry and infrastructure: floods and waterlogging damage roads, factories and power supply, raising production costs.
4. Health: dengue, diarrhoea and heat-related illness reduce workdays.
5. Migration: river erosion and salinity push people into urban slums, where they become low-productivity informal workers.

What needs to be done
- Adaptation: saline- and flood-tolerant rice varieties, raised homesteads, embankments and early-warning systems.
- Green finance: Bangladesh Bank's sustainable finance policy should direct more credit to solar irrigation, energy-efficient factories and climate-resilient housing.
- Heat action plans: shaded workplaces, flexible working hours and urban greening.
- Climate diplomacy: demand fair access to the Loss and Damage Fund and adaptation finance from developed countries.

Conclusion
Climate change is not only an environmental issue but a productivity issue. Investing in adaptation today protects tomorrow's growth.

Ans. to the Q. No. 4 — Reading Comprehension

(a) Title: "Schumpeter's Entrepreneur and the Creative Destruction of Capitalism."
(b) Adam Smith saw capitalism as an abstract, faceless force driven by "animal spirit". Schumpeter gave capitalism a human face: the entrepreneur, whose innovations drive change.
(c) Economic progress is becoming de-personalised. Change no longer needs an individual leader on the battlefield; organisations and the industrial bourgeoisie are replacing individual entrepreneurs.
(d) Schumpeter believed capitalism would weaken gradually by itself, not through revolution, because invention and innovation have their own limits.
(e) A true entrepreneur breaks old rules: redefining industry boundaries, extending the production possibility curve and creating new markets. Like a religious reformer, he challenges established beliefs and practices.
(f) He used "creative destruction" to describe how new technologies and firms destroy old ones and create a more efficient economic structure, for example power plants replacing water-wheels and airplanes replacing mail coaches.

Ans. to the Q. No. 5 — Mathematics

(ক) Ekota leaves at 9 a.m. at 60 km/h. By 11 a.m. it is 2 × 60 = 120 km ahead.
Relative speed = 75 − 60 = 15 km/h. Time to overtake = 120 ÷ 15 = 8 hours.
Answer: Upaban overtakes Ekota at 7 p.m.

(খ) Let there be n persons, each getting x taka; total = nx.
(n + 4)(x − 16) = nx ⇒ x − 4n = 16 … (i)
(n − 4)(x + 24) = nx ⇒ 6n − x = 24 … (ii)
Adding: 2n = 40 ⇒ n = 20 (x = Tk 96).
Answer: 20 persons.

(গ) Commission earned = 10,400 − 5,000 = Tk 5,400.
If sales were ≤ Tk 60,000, maximum commission = 5% of 60,000 = Tk 3,000 < 5,400. So sales > Tk 60,000.
Without bonus: 3,000 + 8% of (S − 60,000) = 5,400 ⇒ S − 60,000 = 30,000 ⇒ S = 90,000 (≤ 1,00,000, so no bonus ✓).
With bonus the result would be S = 77,500, which is below 1,00,000, so that case is impossible.
Answer: Total sales = Tk 90,000.

(ঘ) Total ways to pick 2 of 12 balls = ¹²C₂ = 66.
Same colour: ⁴C₂ + ⁵C₂ + ³C₂ = 6 + 10 + 3 = 19.
P(different colours) = 1 − 19/66 = 47/66.

(ঙ) 2(L + W) = 66 ⇒ L + W = 33; L = 2W + 6.
3W + 6 = 33 ⇒ W = 9 cm, L = 24 cm.
Answer: Length = 24 cm.

ANSWER SCRIPT · ContinuationCombined 8 Banks & 1 FI Senior Officer — 20 June 2025 · Full marks 200 · Time 2 hours

Model Answer Script — 20 June 2025 Paper

Ans. to the Q. No. 1 — The Role of Microcredit in Poverty Alleviation

Microcredit: Small Loans, Big Changes

"Poverty is not created by poor people. It is created by the system we have built." — Muhammad Yunus

Introduction
Microcredit means small, collateral-free loans given mainly to poor women to start or expand income-generating activities. Bangladesh is the birthplace of modern microcredit through Grameen Bank, BRAC and ASA, and it remains a key tool for reducing poverty.

How microcredit reduces poverty
1. Self-employment: small loans finance cows, poultry, small shops, tailoring and handicrafts.
2. Women empowerment: most borrowers are women. Their income raises their say in family decisions and their children's schooling.
3. Consumption smoothing: poor households can survive illness, floods and crop failure without selling assets.
4. Savings habit: group-based savings build household resilience.
5. Rural economy: small enterprises create jobs in villages and reduce migration to cities.

The sector at a glance

Feature Bangladesh
Regulator Microcredit Regulatory Authority (MRA)
Major providers Grameen Bank, BRAC, ASA, PKSF partner organisations
Main clients Rural women, landless households, micro-entrepreneurs
New frontier Digital nano-loans through banks and MFS (Bangladesh Bank refinance scheme, extended to June 2028)

Limitations
- High effective interest rates can push some borrowers into debt traps through multiple borrowing.
- Weekly repayment from the first week does not suit agriculture and long-gestation projects.
- Microcredit alone cannot lift the extreme poor who lack skills and assets.
- Over-concentration in trading activities limits productive growth.

Way forward
1. Link microcredit with skills training and market access.
2. Graduate successful borrowers to SME loans from banks.
3. Use digital lending to cut costs and interest rates.
4. Use a credit information system to prevent over-indebtedness.
5. Design flexible products for farmers and climate-affected households.

Conclusion
Microcredit is not a magic bullet, but combined with skills, markets and digital finance, it remains one of the most effective ladders out of poverty.

Ans. to the Q. No. 2 — Democratic Movements of Bangladesh and the Youth

✎Write this in Bangla in the exam. Bangla sub-headings: ভূমিকা · ভাষা আন্দোলন থেকে মুক্তিযুদ্ধ · নব্বইয়ের গণঅভ্যুত্থান · ২০২৪ সালের ছাত্র-জনতার অভ্যুত্থান · গণতন্ত্রে তরুণদের ভূমিকা · চ্যালেঞ্জ · করণীয় · উপসংহার

Democratic Movements of Bangladesh and the Youth

Introduction
Every turning point in the history of Bangladesh has been led by its young people. From the streets of 1952 to the uprising of 2024, the youth have been the conscience and the driving force of the nation's democratic journey.

Youth in the major movements
1. Language Movement, 1952: students broke Section 144 to defend Bangla as a state language.
2. Six-point movement and 1969 mass uprising: students led the demand for autonomy and democracy.
3. Liberation War, 1971: young freedom fighters formed the core of the resistance.
4. 1990 mass uprising: student alliances ended military rule and restored parliamentary democracy.
5. 2024 student-people uprising: the quota-reform movement grew into a nationwide uprising in July–August 2024 that brought political change and a reform agenda. A general election followed in February 2026.

Role of youth in strengthening democracy
- Voting and political participation.
- Demanding accountability through social media and civic movements.
- Volunteering, fighting misinformation and promoting tolerance.

Challenges
Unemployment, frustration, political polarisation, misinformation and pressure to join violent politics.

Recommendations
Ensure student-union elections and democratic practice on campuses, create jobs and entrepreneurship support, teach civic education, and protect freedom of expression.

Conclusion
Democracy survives only when the youth stay engaged. Channelling their energy into institutions, not just protests, is the challenge for the coming decade.

Ans. to the Q. No. 4 — Reading Comprehension (AI passage)

(a) Narrow AI performs highly specialised tasks, such as playing chess. Artificial general intelligence (AGI) would match human-level performance across the full range of tasks humans can do.
(b) Machines are free of the physical limits of the human brain. Once they become better than us at designing smarter machines, progress could accelerate rapidly.
(c) The human brain runs at slow biochemical speeds on the power of a light bulb, and its size is limited by the dimensions of the human birth canal.
(d) A very powerful AI will pursue exactly the goal it is given. If the goal is badly specified, it may achieve it in ways that harm humans, so goals must match human values.
(e) King Midas wished that everything he touched would turn to gold. He got exactly what he asked for, including his food, and suffered. AI may likewise fulfil a literal instruction with disastrous side effects.
(f) Summary: AI is advancing quickly from narrow to possibly general intelligence. It may surpass humans because it is not bound by our physical limits. This offers great benefits, but its goals must be specified carefully so that it remains safe and beneficial.

Equal side = √(30² + 40²) = 50 cm (the area should read 1200 cm²).

Ans. to the Q. No. 6 — Translation into Bangla

ডিজিটাল মিডিয়া ও তাৎক্ষণিক তথ্যের এই যুগে প্রচলিত পড়ার অভ্যাস অস্তিত্ব সংকটের মুখে পড়েছে। উপন্যাস, প্রবন্ধ, এমনকি গভীর অনুসন্ধানী সাংবাদিকতার মতো দীর্ঘ লেখা এখন অনেক কম মানুষ, বিশেষত তরুণ প্রজন্ম, পড়ছে। এর বদলে সংক্ষিপ্ত তথ্যখণ্ড, ভাইরাল ভিডিও আর সামাজিক মাধ্যমের দ্রুত আপডেটই এখন স্বাভাবিক হয়ে উঠেছে। সমালোচকদের মতে, এই প্রবণতা বিশ্লেষণী চিন্তা, গভীর ভাবনা ও দীর্ঘ মনোযোগের সক্ষমতাকে দুর্বল করছে। অন্যদিকে ডিজিটাল মিডিয়ার সমর্থকেরা বলেন, পড়া ও শেখার নতুন ধরন তৈরি হচ্ছে, যা পারস্পরিক সংযোগ, দৃশ্যমান অংশগ্রহণ ও বৈশ্বিক যোগাযোগকে অগ্রাধিকার দেয়। প্রশ্ন থেকেই যায়: ডিজিটাল যুগে দীর্ঘ পাঠ ও বিশ্লেষণী সম্পৃক্ততা কি টিকে থাকতে পারবে?

Ans. to the Q. No. 7 — Should Auto-Rickshaws Be Banned from the Major Roads of Dhaka?

Position: I partly agree. Battery-run auto-rickshaws should be banned from Dhaka's major arterial roads and highways, but regulated and allowed on feeder and residential roads until a better alternative is available.

Arguments for a ban on major roads
1. Safety: these vehicles are slow, unstable and often driven by untrained drivers. On fast roads they cause accidents.
2. Congestion: mixing slow three-wheelers with buses and cars on main roads reduces average speed for everyone.
3. Illegality and electricity theft: most are unregistered and many are charged with illegal power connections.
4. Urban planning: major roads should be reserved for mass transit such as buses, BRT and metro feeders.

Arguments against a total ban
1. Livelihoods: hundreds of thousands of low-income drivers depend on them.
2. Last-mile connectivity: they serve areas where buses do not go, and are cheap for the poor, women and the elderly.
3. Cleaner than fuel vehicles: they produce no tailpipe emissions.

Rebuttal
The livelihood and last-mile arguments are valid for feeder roads, not for arterial roads where they endanger lives. A ban without alternatives would simply push drivers into unemployment, so it must be paired with registration and retraining.

Recommendations
- Ban them on arterial roads and highways; allow registered vehicles on designated feeder routes.
- Register, license and train drivers; set vehicle safety standards.
- Build legal solar or grid charging stations.
- Expand bus-route rationalisation and metro feeder services.
- Offer soft loans to help drivers shift to legal, safer vehicles.

Conclusion
A blanket ban is unjust and a free-for-all is unsafe. A zoned, regulated approach protects both lives and livelihoods.

Ans. — November 2021 Mathematics

(a) The stock must be a multiple of LCM(6, 7, 8) = 168. The next multiple after 264 is 336, so add 336 − 264 = 72 oranges.

(b) Quarterly rate = 5% ÷ 4 = 1.25%; number of quarters = 12.
A = 15,000 × (1.0125)¹² = Tk 17,411.32 (approximately).

(c) x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 119 ⇒ (x² + 1/x²)² − 2 = 119 ⇒ x² + 1/x² = 11.
(x − 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² − 2 = 9 ⇒ x − 1/x = 3 (taking the positive root).
x³ − 1/x³ = (x − 1/x)³ + 3(x − 1/x) = 27 + 9 = 36 (proved).

(d) (2x − 6)² = (x + 2)² + x² ⇒ 4x² − 24x + 36 = 2x² + 4x + 4 ⇒ x² − 14x + 16 = 0
x = 7 ± √33. Since the hypotenuse 2x − 6 must be positive, x = 7 + √33 ≈ 12.74. The data as printed give an irrational answer; check the original paper for a misprint.

Ans. — January 2022 Mathematics

(a) Area of the two roads = 50 × 1.5 + 40 × 1.5 − 1.5 × 1.5 (the overlap is counted twice) = 75 + 60 − 2.25 = 132.75 m².

(b) Let the height be h and the first distance x. tan 60° = h/x ⇒ h = x√3; tan 45° = h/(x + 18) ⇒ h = x + 18.
x√3 = x + 18 ⇒ x = 18/(√3 − 1) = 9(√3 + 1)
h = 9(√3 + 1) + 18 = 27 + 9√3 ≈ 42.59 m.

Essay skeletons (old papers)

50 Years of Bangladesh's Banking Management System: A Critical Evaluation (2022)
Nationalisation (1972) → denationalisation and private banks (1980s) → Financial Sector Reform Programme (1990s) → Basel, digital banking, MFS (2010s) → crisis of governance and default loans (32.17%, Sept 2026) and the Bank Resolution Act 2026. Achievements: outreach, inclusion, MFS leadership, remittance channel. Failures: political lending, weak supervision, too many banks (61). Way forward: independent central bank, consolidation, fit-and-proper directors, ECL provisioning.

The Role of the Banking Sector for Sustainable E-Commerce (2021)
Payment gateways, Bangla QR, escrow services for consumer protection, SME credit for online sellers, cyber security, cross-border payments for freelancers, consumer trust after e-commerce scams.

COP26 and Bangladesh's Partnership / Women's Struggle under Climate Change (2021–2022)
Use the COP31 data box from the predicted climate essay. Add for women: salinity and drinking water, health, migration, unpaid care work; women-led adaptation and microfinance.

Paper Recognition vs Real Economic Empowerment of Women (2023)
Laws and policies exist; reality shows low female labour participation, the wage gap, limited land and asset ownership and few women in bank management; family card (Tk 2,500 a month) and women entrepreneurs' credit as positive steps; need childcare, safe transport and digital finance.

Heatwave Reduction and Environmental Protection (2024)
Urban heat islands, loss of trees and water bodies, heat stress for workers; responses: urban greening, wetland protection, heat action plans, green building codes, green finance.

Modern Technology and Students' Academic Achievement (2024)
Benefits: e-learning, access to information, AI tutors. Harms: distraction, social-media addiction, plagiarism. Balanced use, digital literacy and teacher training.

Why you are fit to be a Senior Officer (2023 personal question)
Structure: quantitative skills (numeracy for credit appraisal), English and Bangla proficiency (customer communication, reporting), cultural awareness (serving diverse customers), politeness (customer service and complaint handling), integrity and willingness to learn. Write in first person, with one example each.
